#3724. Blade Runner 2099 bosses hint at a possible "triple-A" Blade Runner game in the future - just don't expect it any time soon

Blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game. And a 'triple-A' video game, at that. At least that's according to Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment (which owns the Blade Runner IP).

In a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope. Other than that, the duo seemed to want to keep any potential information to themselves. Given they appear to be in talks about the title, rather than in any active development, if something did come of this ideation, it would no doubt be a long, long way off. Kosove and Johnson's aim seems to be getting players to "interact" more with the world of Blade Runner, which has recently been fleshed out by the 2017 movie and is set to be developed more in the upcoming series.

Of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before. There was 1997's simply-titled Blade Runner - developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive - which was a point-and-click adventure that really seemed to pick up the vibes the original Ridley Scott was putting down. An Enhanced Edition of the game was released in 2022, which is actually more of a remake than a simple enhancement.

Then, in 2023, Annapurna Interactive unveiled its very first internally-developed game, in the form of Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth. The game, which promised to riff on the dystopian universe established in Ridley Scott's cult classic movie, would have been sandwiched squarely between that film and its sequel, Blade Runner 2049. It was going to be set in LA after the Blackout hits, but beyond that - and the fact it's coming to PC and consoles at some point - few details ever managed to break through the PR barrier before the game went dark: it's been removed from Annapurna's website and delisted from Steam. Curious.

If you want to see something more from the cyberpunk world sooner, Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on 25th November.

Johnny Depp’s transformation into Ebenezer is chilling (it even terrified Sam Claflin, who plays Ebenezer’s nephew, Fred), and him throwing out his signature “bah humbug” is intimidating. At the start of Ti West’s take on A Christmas Carol, it’s hard to imagine the grouchy character being capable of saying “Merry Christmas.” So, when he actually does say it at the end of the movie, it makes a big impact. With that in mind, I asked Claflin, who was on the receiving end of the jolly statement, what it meant to hear those words said by Ebenezer Scrooge.

At the end of Ebenezer, after the titular character has been visited by the ghosts and realized his wrongs, he works to redeem himself. He gives Bob Cratchit a much-deserved promotion, he gives a beggar his pocket watch, and he finally goes to see his nephew Fred to apologize and say Merry Christmas. When Claflin was speaking with director Ti West about playing Fred in this book-to-screen adaptation, he didn’t fully get the importance of his character; however, he told me that he quickly realized not only the significance of Fred, but the significance of this moment. He explained:

Well, in all honesty, when I was first talking to Ti about the script, and he sort of said ‘I was thinking of you to play the part Fred,’ I was like, ‘Who's Fred?’ For some reason, that role, that character, had never really resonated with me, or I'd never really taken notice of it. But especially the way that Ti wanted to kind of really focus on that within this version of the story, he really kind of felt like it added so much depth and gave the film even more heart.

Throughout Ebenezer, all Fred wants is for Ebenezer to be happy and to maintain one relationship that ties them both back to Fred’s mom and Ebenezer’s sister. He wants his uncle to be part of the family, and he keeps going back to him over and over again to invite him into his home for the holidays.

Claflin said he “really understood Fred’s objective” and why he was so adamant about keeping Depp’s character in his life. He also explained the lessons we can learn from this relationship, and the way it ends with Ebenezer saying “Merry Christmas.” Telling me why his character’s journey and mission to keep the titular character in his life is so important, the Catching Fire actor explained:

I think it's important to kind of not give up hope on the people that feel like they've lost. You know, it'd be so easy to give up and to move on. But I think the fact that he is just so determined and so true and almost desperate with his love – but it pays to be kind, and it pays to be generous, and it pays to be thoughtful and understanding and loving, and you know, Fred is a great example of how the world should be, really.

I totally agree. Fred’s motivations are so pure and rooted in deep familial love. His way of looking at the world is something worth striving for, and his inability to give up on his family is admirable. Clearly, it works in a way, too, because Ebenezer does come back to him. He does accept the love Fred so desperately wants to give, and they’re able to be a family. That all makes the “Merry Christmas” mean more, as Claflin told me:

Yeah, it was an honor to hear those words uttered from Ebenezer's mouth.

While Ebenezer has gotten mixed reviews, I enjoyed it. And I particularly loved the ending, and seeing Ebenezer realize why life’s worth living. Seeing him bring love back into his life, and feeling that lovely holiday spirit, brought me joy, and clearly it brought Fred and Sam Claflin joy too.

Now, if you’d like to see Ebenezer, you can catch this new take on A Christmas Carol in theaters now.

#3722. Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

#3721. Treyarch lays off lead Call of Duty writer and Zombies veteran after "approximately 20 years" of service

"Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years."

Treyarch's former Senior lead writer, Craig Houston, has been laid off after approximately 20 years of service with the developer. In a post made to both his Twitter/X account and LinkedIn, the developer thanked fans for their support during his two decades with the company and confirmed he was impacted by recent reorganistation within the studio.

"After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts. "I am proud to have worked with so many talented people - many of whom will remain friends for life. Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years."

On Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message. It appears the layoffs referenced are part of the broad reorganistation affecting 3200 jobs that Xbox announced earlier this year. Treyarch, as part of Activision Blizzard, is owned by Xbox.

Houston is a bonafide veteran of the esteemed FPS series. His first Call of Duty title at Treyarch was Call of Duty 3, where he worked as a video editor. This was followed by World at War, Black Ops 1 through 4, where he is credited as a writer and designer. For Modern Warfare, Black Ops - Cold War, Vanguard, Modern Warfare 3, then Black Ops 6 and 7, he is listed as a member of the design team and in 'creative development'. He is not credited on this year's Modern Warfare 4.

If you've picked up a Call of Duty game in the past decade-plus, you'll have interacted with Houston's work: he was a central creative force behind the writing for Treyarch's campaign modes since 2006 (with Call of Duty 3) and the main writer for the Zombies mode since 2008 (with Call of Duty: World at War). Alongside Jimmy Zielinski, Jason Blundell, and Kevin Drew, Houston was an integral part of the evolution of the Zombies pillar of Call of Duty, and shaped it into the series-defining thing it is today. There has been a fair amount of community support for Houston since he announced the news yesterday; he was a popular dev, and a lot of the Zombies-specific fan communities online hold a lot of respect for him.

"Craig is a great guy," notes one user on Reddit. "You can tell how much he loves the story/characters he writes just by how excited he is when he talks about them in promo material."

"You're a Legend Craig, it was an honor to work with you," says ex-Treyarch vet, Tony Flame, in a reply to Houston's X post. "You created a truly special experience that will live on in the kinds of millions fans. Wishing you the best [...]."

From all of us here at Eurogamer, and myself personally - who really admires the character-work and emergent storytelling present in the Xbox 360-era Call of Duty games, specifically - we wish you the best and good luck with the future, Craig.

"This is just objectively so much more expensive, so much more time-consuming"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Until last month, Exodus' adoption of the mantle of 'Mass Effect spiritual successor' had been relatively gradual. As a party-based sci-fi RPG made by BioWare veterans, the comparison was inevitable, but it wasn't until the sudden closure of BioWare and cancelation of Mass Effect 5 that Exodus became the sole means by which that lineage would be continued. For its leading voice actors, announced today, that means being thrust into the limelight with perhaps a little more attention being paid than they were expecting.

As with Mass Effect's Commander Shepard, Exodus' lead character, Jun Aslan, will be playable as either a male or female character. Male Jun will be played by Stephen Oyoung, who has a handful of performance capture roles, most notably as Martin Li / Mr Negative in the Marvel's Spider-Man games. Carina Conti, who plays the female version of Jun, had her first and only video game role as Isabella Torrisi in last year's Mafia: The Old Country. But for both actors, the realities of shooting a sprawling, choice-based RPG offer a new challenge as performers.

"When you're in the volume with a linear game," Oyoung explains, "you're just shooting the scene as it is." But with Exodus, production had a choice to make: Do you "shoot an entire path and then go back" to where different parts of the story branch away from one another, or "stop, and [...] literally have to physically map out where we are"? Archetype chose the latter option, but Conti says that even without having to retrace their steps over and over, the process was "much harder" than their previous role.

"There were so many times in the recording process where I said 'I can't believe they chose to do this'," she says. "This is just objectively so much more expensive, so much more time-consuming, so much more complicated." That complexity, from a performer's standpoint, stems not just from holding together multiple branches of a story, but from having to wind back the clock to entire dialogue choices or even character perspectives that are entirely different from the previous scene. Exodus' morality system frames choices as either Paladin or Immortal paths, something that Conti says "was a really unique challenge" to record.

"You have to flip from recording one version of reality to another version of reality where you don't feel the way that you did in the first one," Conti says. But that challenge is one that both actors rose to: "I think as actors, you're always doing that," says Oyoung. "The wonderful thing was that you could say the [line], and then there is that other thing that you wanted to say as well, and you get that opportunity to play it." For Conti, the process was "exactly what it means to be able to take a note. You've created the character within yourself - you know what you yourself would naturally default to doing, but then you have to be willing to take the director's input, a note from creative, and you have to be willing to accept that this character is going to do something other than what you had originally decided."

That rewriting of realities is true of most RPGs, but Exodus presented an additional challenge for Conti and Oyoung: Time Dilation. As Jun jets off to distant corners of the galaxy at FTL speeds, time will pass more quickly for the friends they leave behind. That means that months or years might go by in what feels like just a few hours for Jun, and the impact of their choices will be felt over years or even decades. Despite the narrative complexity that offers, however, both Juns seemed to think they had the easier job as performers.

"I often joked with all of the other actors because they'd say to me 'you've got a tough job, you're in every scene'," says Oyoung. But his feelings were the opposite: "Most of them change a lot because of time dilation. Whereas, as Jun, our toughest job was just to react with the proper emotion to that time change." Conti agrees - "It's much harder when you have to come up with all of the story of your life and the time that has passed on your own. We were lucky enough to have been fed all of the events, step-by-step. There are so many moments in the game that really shape Jun as a person, and we get to play all of that first-hand [...] whereas all of the other characters who might get left behind, we don't necessarily get to see all of the trials they're put through. And so those actors have to do all that work on their own, and decide how that changes the character. I think they had the much harder job."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

It's not just the supporting cast putting their own spin on a character, though. Conti and Oyoung say their respective versions of Jun have their own "flavor," helped in part by the fact that they never met to talk about the character on set. In fact, Conti spent days looking for Oyoung on set, expecting to see the male version of Jun looking back at her in the hallways, but he was never there. Oyoung recorded first, and cutscenes that were rendered around his performance meant that sometimes, Conti had to match his movements. But even so, she says "I would find it impossible to recreate exactly what Stephen did."

Exactly how Conti's version of Jun differs from Oyoung's is hard to tell - today's new trailer is our first look at Archetype's female lead, and a short video can never hope to capture the depth of a full-length RPG. But the pair are leaning into their differences; "Fundamentally we have different perspectives, but the sum of what makes up an actor will always translate differently," Conti says, inadvertently touching on the varying timelines and galaxies that will likely mean no two Exodus playthroughs will feel the same: "This is why you get a million different incredible versions of Hamlet, and you can keep watching it because it will continue to be different and contain multitudes and universes that the other actor couldn't bring."

#3718. Unity launches new Fellowship program, offering a "no recoup" $50,000 grant to indie developers planning to launch their game in the next 12 months

Unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the company has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

The Damon/Kimmel faux feud has been going on for decades at this point, and it just never gets old. Matt Damon and Jimmy Kimmel have been pretending to hate each other for years, doing bits about it at the Oscars and on Kimmel’s talk show. And despite actually being great friends, they love to keep this bit going. On that note, the talk show host was recently asked to give a toast to Matt Damon at a huge Hollywood event, and there's a hilarious video that I just can't get enough of!

Damon has had quite a year, having released The Rip, which co-stars his best friend, Ben Affleck. The Rip was also a huge hit for Netflix and allowed for him to continue to work with Affleck amid other projects at their production company. Damon was also most notably the star of The Odyssey, which grossed well over a billion dollars worldwide and is an awards season favorite. As a result, GQ named Damon one of their Men of the Year in their annual issue. At the party to celebrate the magazine. Jimmy Kimmel gave quite the speech, which you can see below:

Kimmel, of course, couldn’t resist mentioning some controversial people named in GQ magazine over the years to compare Damon, too. On top of that, the talk show was quick to say that Tom Holland was more deserving of this honor. Kimmel said:

Matt had a big year and he's in great company. I've made a list of some of the other honorees. Mel Gibson, 1996, 2007, Kanye West. The list goes on and on and you you deserve it. You really do. Not as much as others might deserve it. You know, Tom Holland was in the Odyssey and Spider-Man this year. He was in number one and number two. You're just number two. You're a big number two. You deserve this.

Kimmel then toasted to his faux foe and fittingly called him “Mrs. Ben Affleck.” Of course, Damon had his own hilarious quips as a response. He was quick to point out one key detail about that night, saying:

I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place.

Of course, this is all in good fun, and the riffing is expected any time these two guys are in the same room together. It started back in the early 2000s when Jimmy Kimmel started saying “Apologies to Matt Damon, we ran out of time” at the end of every show. It was a self-deprecating joke, as a way to make fun of how terrible his guests were when his show first started, as opposed to having a movie star like Damon. It became a running joke that continued even as Kimmel’s show became more successful.

Periodically, Damon tries to sneak onto Kimmel’s show, and the host jokingly refuses to have the actor on as a guest. They also make fun of each other relentlessly in public, and hilariously compete for the affection of Ben Affleck. It’s a great bit, and if this GQ speech is any indication, this duo isn’t planning on retiring the quips anytime soon. I hope they continue to dig at each other for years to come, because it is just too much fun to watch.

Fans can check out Matt Damon in The Odyssey, which is still playing in select theaters nationwide. It’s the tail end of The Odyssey’s historic box office run, so make sure to see it on the big screen while you still can. You can also watch Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which airs at 11:35 p.m. ET on ABC and is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3716. Cyberpunk 2077 mod Torrent adds 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City

A new Cyberpunk 2077 mod has overhauled Night City's rain, swapping the game's flat wet weather effects for individual 3D drops and adding lightning storms.

As spotted by DSOGaming, modder CyanideX's mod, Torrent, gives each raindrop its own size and falling speed. The drops also react to the player's movement, so they stream towards the windscreen when you're driving fast. If you find the wind has picked up, blustery weather can also push them sideways, too.

The rain also catches the light from street lamps, neon signs, car headlights, and taillights, and won't fall through roofs or inside buildings. Drops splash on the ground, heavy rain leaves mist in the distance, and cars throw up spray from their tyres on wet roads.

The mod complements this with a new lightning system, with branching bolts that flash and flicker before fading, and that can arrive in bursts during heavier storms.

If you like a little lightning, the frequency of bolts can be adjusted across 10 levels, and with the AudioXL mod installed, thunder follows each strike, timed to how far away it landed.

For players sensitive to flashing lights, a Reduce Flashes option dims the lightning, replaces its flicker with a single slow glow, and halves the number of strikes.

Torrent supports Nova City 2 and other weather mods, and adds extra storm effects for Nova City 2 players, including mist that rolls through the streets with the wind. It’s available now on Nexus Mods.

The US president doesn't seem too concerned about the potential risks to US national security: "I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A CNBC report says the return of disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang is not being considered by Nvidia's board of directors, despite a rising chorus of billionaire voices calling for it—including, earlier today, that of US president Donald Trump.

"I would not mind. I would not mind that," Trump told reporters in response to a question about Huang's possible return (via Reuters). "I like—I threw out the name of Tim Cook. But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement—I think he learned a big lesson, I guess. Maybe one lesson's more important than another. But I would certainly not mind seeing that."

Asked about US intelligence reports that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Trump said he doesn't know whether she's a spy, and that "a lot of people" are asking Huang to return to the CEO's role.

"They think Jensen should go back," Trump said. "That certainly isn't a bad idea." He also said that US national security was not put at risk by Huang's deep ties to Trump, adding that "China plays games with us, so we play games with China."

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, shortly after his affairs with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence as well as multiple Nvidia employees came to light. Calls for his return were almost immediate, mostly notably from billionaires like Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, but also Nvidia employees and fans. Tech executives have reportedly launched a "war room" to lobby for his return, and Huang himself is apparently open to the idea.

Whether Nvidia feels the same is another matter: An anonymous source told CNBC that the board is not considering bringing him back, and is instead focusing on an investigation into Huang's affairs and whether he compromised US national security or Nvidia itself.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, one of Trump's most vocal and reliable supporters, also recently seemed to dismiss the idea, saying Nvidia "needed a dramatic shakeup" at the top and that it should look "outside the company" for a new chief executive. It remains to be seen whether any of those positions change in light of Trump's support.

The GTA 6 release time is almost here, signifying the end of more than a decade of waiting and finally giving us the opportunity to set foot in Leonida so we can explore Vice City and beyond. November 19, 2026 will be etched into players' memories for the launch of GTA 6, and while the official release time is set for midnight locally on that date there are some potential variations to be aware of. Get yourself prepared for the GTA 6 side activities we know about so far, and find out which GTA 6 animals you're likely to encounter on your travels.

The GTA 6 release time on PS5 is Thursday, November 19 at midnight local time in your region, as there are individual PlayStation Stores for each region with their own time settings and your access will be based on which Store you purchased the game from. However, our own testing shows the US PSN Store has the release time set to midnight EST, which equates to 9pm PST on Wednesday, November 18 – it's unclear if there is further time zone correction across the US, so check the Store page to confirm what local time is displayed for you.

While the GTA 6 release time on Xbox is also Thursday, November 19 at midnight local time in your region, Xbox operates a single global store which means you can potentially get earlier access by changing the time zone on your console. We've got a separate guide on how to play GTA 6 early using the New Zealand time zone method, which would let you start playing at the following times:

However you access it, you'll need to make sure you've completed the GTA 6 preload in advance so you have everything ready to go, and that may involved deleting other content off your hard drive to make room for the GTA 6 GB size of up to 212GB depending on your platform.

#3713. Police arrest suspect after drive-by shooting at office campus housing Xbox studio inXile

Police are still investigating the motive.

Police have arrested a suspect after a drive-by shooting at an office campus in Tustin, California, which is home to Xbox-owned studio inXile Entertainment.

According to Aftermath, officers responded to reports of a drive-by shooting at Flight at Tustin Legacy, a campus that houses inXile and other businesses, on 11th November.

"Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt," Tustin Police Sergeant Christopher Peterson told the outlet. "Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We're relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," an inXile spokesperson said. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

Police have not given a motive, and the suspect has not been named.

InXile is the studio behind the Wasteland series, and is currently working on Clockwork Revolution.

#3712. "Games are best made by people": The IWGB and other European unions publish joint manifesto calling on workers, employers and consumers to reject genAI

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people."

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture."

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games."

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable."

Plenty of films left impressions on the 2026 movie schedule, but few managed to really hit the zeitgeist like Project Hail Mary did. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s science-fiction epic – based on Andy Weir’s 2021 book of the same name – managed to capture audiences’ imaginations (and make some solid money at the box office in the process). Anyone who needs further proof of the film’s popularity should know that a mixed-reality game is in the works and, to quote Rocky, the description of his role sounds “amaze.”

This new game – Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars – hails from game studio Maze Theory and takes place during a formerly untapped period of time within the main story. It specifically takes place after Dr. Ryland Grace saves his alien companion, Rocky, and before they return to the latter’s homeworld, Enid. Players take on the role of Dr. Ryland Grace (played by the impeccable and expressive Ryan Gosling in the film) and, as SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend learned from the developers, the game gets quite immersive.

Players can interact with objects, steer the titular ship (Hail Mary), repair it and even complete tasks like opening cupboards. One also only needs a headset to further immerse themselves in the game’s story, which was also talked out with Weir. Of course, all the while, fans can also interact with Rocky (who is not a pet) throughout their travels, and he’ll be actively watching your moves and providing feedback. Gameplay lead Sandy Lockie told SFX this about bringing Rocky and Grace’s relationship to the game:

We wanted to do justice to Rocky and Grace and their relationship. Sometimes they’ll be crabby with each other, sometimes they’ll get a little bit down and need the other one to pick them up.

It just wouldn’t have made sense to craft a game like this without including Rocky in some form or fashion. Since the film’s release he’s become something of a sensation, and he went viral after Amazon posted a video of the character watching himself. Even Neil DeGrasse Tyson praised the character’s design and noted that Weir and the filmmakers avoid the Hollywood trope of making him a humanoid. Judging by Lockie’s comments, even the Maze Theory team was taken with Rocky while they were testing the game:

Even when we’re testing, although you know he’s a character and isn’t really there, I’ll talk to him: ‘Well, what do I do here?’ He has good suggestions and sometimes bad suggestions. It’s one of those things that your brain just kind of lunges into, like, ‘Yep, Rocky’s there. He’s a character now!’ He’ll do jazz hands or prompt you to play rock-paper-scissors and all sorts of stuff . It’s fun to step into that and feel like he’s your friend and companion, your little explorer buddy.

All in all, this game should provide fans with a bit of a taste of being in Ryland’s shoes and present the opportunity to catch up with Rocky in some sense. Project Hail Mary’s ending may have closed the book on Grace and Rocky’s bromance for now, but I still like the idea of people being able to create their own moments reminiscent of the film’s best scenes. So, on that note, why not jump into this sweet-sounding extension of the PHM story?

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is now available Pico, Meta and Android XR. Also, fans can grab a Prime Video subscription and stream the movie on which the game is based right now.

#3710. EA hires another former Call of Duty boss to take the lead on all Battlefield Studios' projects

EA has made some notable leadership changes within its studios group, and in who oversees the Battlefield franchise. Byron Beede, previously Battlefield's general manager, has been promoted to group general manager.

Beede announced the change on LinkedIn, saying that he now oversees EA's shooter and action-RPG portfolio, seemingly occupying the role of the late Vince Zampella.

In this stead, EA appointed Sam Cooper as Battlefield's new boss. Cooper, who also revealed his new job title on LinkedIn, previously had a stint at EA Sports, but he's mostly known for his work at Activision, where he spent the last five-ish years as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

While this might seem like fairly unremarkable corporate news - executives move between rival companies all the time, after all - it reinforces a narrative that EA continues to keenly replicate Activision's Call of Duty model.

That particular push is years-old now, and it kicked off in 2021 when EA hired Byron Beede, former boss of all of Call of Duty at Activision, to lead the next evolution of Battlefield. So far, that decision has given us the very successful Battlefield 6 and its free-to-play, COD: Warzone-like battle royale mode Redsec.

To facilitate that, EA rearranged several of its studios to serve under one banner dubbed Battlefield Studios, replicating Activision's model of locking several teams around the world into developing and supporting a single game / franchise. Ripple Effect, Motive, the iconic Criterion and, of course, series creator DICE are all the Battlefield franchise's lead and support studios.

Many players argue - and I would agree - that Battlefield and Call of Duty games are more alike today than they've ever been. The user interface, the emphasis on limited-time events, the garish store cosmetics, the COD-like battle pass system - complete with a more expensive option, are all signs of that transition. And that is to say nothing of controversial changes to longstanding Battlefield tenets, such as the class system, intended to make Battlefield 6 appeal to a wider audience.

The effects of that leadership change likely won't materialise until the next Battlefield title, but it's a curious one to keep in mind as EA leans even harder into its biggest franchises following its $55bn private equity and Saudi Arabia's PIF-funded buyout.

#3709. I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

The latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

The crew retention on Newell's boats is six times the average on other superyachts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leviathan, the 111-meter superyacht owned by Valve co-founder Gabe Newell, has a number of unconventional features. It has a pool for SCUBA testing. It has an NBA-regulation basketball court. An Aston-Martin can be found parked on its helipad. It forgoes the typical teakwood deck in favor of easier-to-clean synthetic flooring.

But for the industry experts at Superyacht Times, which recently released a walkthrough video of the Leviathan's features and operating philosophy (via GamesRadar), the most remarkable thing about Newell's roving wave-palace is its owner's willingness to appreciate the crew that enables his lifestyle of seaborne excess.

"The most surprising thing is what happens when we go through these doors," says Superyacht Times editor-in-chief Francesca Webster as she enters into an immaculate communal dining space on the Leviathan's main deck. "Rather than having the traditional saloon which we normally see on a superyacht—welcoming guests and being the first point of contact to the interior—Gabe actually opted to utilize this incredible space for the crew mess."

Instead of banishing his crew to whatever dank closets and canned rat-gruel might be typical for superyacht staff, Newell enjoys his meals alongside the crew each day. According to Superyacht Times, engaging in that sort of mutual humanity makes him a peculiarity among yachtfolk.

"It's all about shared experience on board his boats. And that is something that we've really never seen before in our industry," Webster says.

Having delivered a casual indictment of the pursuit of yachting in its entirety, we move on the Leviathan's owner deck, where we're shown one of a series of VIP cabins that would shame a top-of-the-line hotel. There, we see more of Newell's uncharacteristic acknowledgment that it would maybe be cool for the people who keep a luxury ship running to enjoy some of the luxury.

"One of the most unique things about Gabe, the ownership structure that he has and the way that he has a vision for yachting," Webster says, "is that this VIP cabin is also used by the crew."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

That vision was apparently a head-scratcher for the vessel's designers at Mark Bryman Design, who Webster says "found this to be quite an incredible challenge and an exciting opportunity to think about yachting from a different perspective and really turn the ownership experience on its head."

Given the video's faintly perplexed tone, Superyacht Times still appears somewhat puzzled by the idea. But the Leviathan's designers seem to have gotten a hold on things eventually: In addition to the crew mess and lavish cabins, the yacht also features a gaming center, outfitted with 15 PCs "for the crew, the guests, and Gabe himself to come and enjoy themselves."

The appreciation evidently goes both ways. Superyacht Times says superyachts retain a crewmember for six to nine months, on average. Newell's crews, however, tend to stay on for an average of four and a half years—a figure that would undoubtedly be lower if he never got over his Mongolian throat singing phase.

#3707. Umamusume: Pretty Derby parent company plans to release seven new games by 2030 as it boasts an "88 percent hit rate" on its mobile titles

Cyberagent - the parent company of Umamusume: Pretty Derby developer Cygames - has boasted its recent successes in the mobile gaming sphere in a recent quarterly earnings presentation.

As part of this presentation (covered by Automaton), the company has established plans to launch seven "major releases" to the mobile platform by 2030. There is no word on what these games will be, but one will be released in 2027, while another two will come in 2028.

Cyberagent boasted an 88 percent "hit" rate for its mobile releases so far, with seven of its eight releases having a development budget of around a billion yen, and reaching a point where it makes that figure back every month from its playerbases. Those games include Umamusume: Pretty Derby, Final Fantasy Ever Crisis, Hololive Dreams, and Jujutsu Kaisen Phantom Parade.

CyberAgent CEO Takahiro Yamauchi - speaking during the presentation - noted that it was still difficult to predict the success of a mobile game ahead of its release. However, he also claims that the experience Cyberagent has gained with its big releases to date have allowed the company to gain a clearer perspective on profitability and sustainability.

This presentation comes after a notable month for Cygmes and Umamusume: Pretty Derby. The developer issued refunds for hotels and flights following the sudden cancellation of an LA live show for the game last month, then shortly after became a major sponsor of the Japanese Formula 1 Grand Prix. The game was also temporarily taken offline due to the major PHP vulnerability exposed last month, an outage that was thankfully short-lived.

#3705. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

While it’s been over three decades since the final Full House episode aired, DJ Tanner actress Candace Cameron Bure still feels her TV “family” is important to her. So, you can only imagine how emotional the TV actress’s tribute was for her TV dad, Bob Saget, on the fourth anniversary of his death this year. If you want to get more in your feels, Bure shared her sweet reaction to BTS footage showing her and Saget on set. Fans, prepare to bring out the tissues.

Since Bob Saget died in 2022 due to accidental blunt head trauma, Candace Cameron Bure said it’s been hard watching Full House clips. But after ET showed her throwback clips from 1994 of her and Saget together on the set of the sitcom (as well as an earlier joint interview with John Stamos), it brought out all kinds of emotional, nostalgic feels:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

I just want to cry seeing the late stand-up comic introduce the former child star as his “TV daughter” as their arms are wrapped around each other. The emotions were already present when the Great American Media actress honored Saget through a series of photos. With each picture, it was clear that Saget didn't need to be Danny Tanner to show affection to his co-stars.

But seeing old clips of Saget with Bure reminded me why they made a great TV father/daughter duo on their show. Their familial chemistry on the ABC series was evident through every heartfelt talk, laugh and of course, hug.

As the former Hallmark Channel star was watching these clips, an emotional Bure revealed it was the first time she had ever seen them. While being “teary-eyed,” the Some Kind of Wonderful alum shared more about what she was thinking while reflecting on the good old days:

That was great! That was so fun to see. [...] Yeah, that was really emotional to see Bob. I just have so much love for him. I really do. He was such a good friend, such a loving person, and loved everyone so well. I miss him. I miss those hugs and the jokes.

The Full House alums truly appeared to have a friendship that stood the test of time. In fact, you could have called their friendship unlikely, as Bure couldn’t get into Saget's raunchy stand-up material. However, she said it was easy to be her TV dad’s friend, as she told herself to separate the comedian’s material from the "kindness" and "love" he brought out. Because the talented actress had known Saget since she was 11, it was no wonder they were still so close by the time the latter passed.

I’m glad that Candace Cameron Bure got to see her younger self with Bob Saget. As heartbreaking as it may be for me to watch those throwback clips, I’d like to believe it strengthens the love and memories she has with her old friend that’ll never go away. You can watch DJ and Danny navigate life together on Full House, which is streaming now with Disney+ subscription or an active Hulu subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3703. The next Xbox, Project Helix, is a console and "not a PC" says Microsoft, as it clarifies that computational power isn't sole focus this time

"It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering."

Microsoft has stressed that its next-generation Xbox console, Project Helix, "is not a PC that can also play console games", but rather "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC". The company has also underlined the importance of using gen-AI-adjacent "neural rendering" technology going forwards, and a desire to remove "all the barriers of play that have historically existed" - notably in making the past generations of games playable.

The details come from a Microsoft-produced Xbox magazine made available digitally yesterday, and a Helix-related feature speaking to Xbox vice president of next generation, Jason Ronald. "When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine," Ronald said, "one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games.

"We're very clear on the design goal," Ronald later added. "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."

Notably, Ronald seemed to suggest that Helix - the console, not the handheld; "Helix" refers to a couple of machines - isn't solely focused on computational grunt. Indeed, he said the next generation wasn't about hitting 8K resolutions and 240 hertz frame-rates, but instead leaning on technologies like "neural rendering" - i.e. generative-AI - and encouraging innovation.

"It's about deeper immersion," Ronald said. "It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering."

While referencing the global component shortage and exorbitant prices of computer hardware, he added: "This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years."

Xbox boss Asha Sharma also recently talked up the importance of generative-AI-sounding technology in Xbox's future, saying "too many ideas never become games", and that "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations".

Another key part of Xbox's Helix vision is compatibility and game preservation. "Game preservation is core to Xbox," Ronald went as far as to say. "Not only do we feel like it's the right thing for the industry, we feel a deep responsibility as one of its biggest platforms and publishers. For the first 30 years of game development, nobody really thought about game preservation when they were designing their hardware, when they were building their games." Xbox is apparently working with game-makers to ensure games can not only be played now but also 20 to 30 years into the future.

The other key facet of Microsoft's push the familiar Play Anywhere mantra, whereby one game can be played across multiple devices, maintaining your game-progress as you go. This is fundamental to Microsoft's handheld-and-console Helix plan, and something we've seen the company dry-run with the Xbox ROG Ally X handheld. "It's this notion that not only does my library move with me, but my progress moves with me as well," Ronald said. "Because I fully expect that when I'm in the middle of an 80-hour RPG, if I'm 25 hours into that and I want to play it on another device, I should be able to instantly resume from where I was. Those are things that today are becoming more common, but I think in the future it's going to be a baseline expectation of all players."

Ronald wouldn't be drawn on the issue of price regarding Project Helix - a recent report suggested Helix could be priced up to $1800 - referring to it only as both "a challenging time" but an "exciting one", because "we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable". Ronald also wouldn't reference a release date, though the report referenced above suggested the handheld Helix machine will release next holiday, 2027, and the console Helix machine the year after. The next generation, then, seems to be around the corner.

#3702. Can GTA 6 make $2 billion in its opening weekend? One industry analyst has run the numbers, and seems to think so

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the company's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

We also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

"That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow."

But it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play."

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

The 007 First Light score is competing with four other videogame soundtracks for the prestigious music industry trophy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Remember that 007 First Light song Lana Del Rey surprised-dropped earlier this year that I said wasn't very good because, as I put it at the time, "it sounds like Bond karaoke"? Well anyway, it's up for a Grammy Award.

The 007 First Light soundtrack, composed by Joe Henson and Alexis Leon Smith, is in the running in the "Best Score Soundtrack For Videogames and Other Interactive Media" category, alongside four other contenders:

To clarify, it's not just the theme song "First Light" that's up for the Grammy, but the full soundtrack—and First Light was not composed by Henson and Smith, but by David Arnold and Lana Del Rey. I assume they're not nominated for the award due to Grammy rules, which require that nominees be "principal artist(s) with significant contributing performances, and/or in-studio producer(s) of a majority of the tracks on the album." A maximum of two album producers and "music supervisors" are eligible to be nominated.

I haven't heard any of the other soundtracks in contention (in my defense, neither Ghost of Yotei nor Wolverine are available on PC, and I actively dislike Star Wars) but after listening to the 007 First Light theme again, and with more time to think about it, I will say this: My initial assessment was absolutely correct.

This is not a good Bond theme. Lana Del Rey may be tremendously talented, but that's lost in the all-consuming effort to hit all the notes without understanding what connects them: The end result is a pale imitation built out of a musical stereotype that's readily identifiable as someone trying really hard to do a Bond theme based on what they were told a Bond theme is supposed to sound like.

The Grammy Awards are a music industry award, not a game award, and that means some games that you might expect to be nominated are sometimes excluded: The rules for the videogame category also state that "videogames that contain music but are not available as stand-alone audio streams/releases" are not eligible for consideration, for example. So if you don't see your favorite of the year in the list, that might be why.

The videogame soundtrack category is relatively new: The Grammy Awards only added it in 2022. Previous winners include:

#3700. Jesen Huang Reportedly Goes From Calling Himself A ‘Piece Of Sh*t’ To Exploring A Return To Nvidia

The dust is still settling from Nvidia’s ousting of founder Jensen Huang over reports of multiple affairs, which allegedly involved two employees at the tech firm. Huang supporters have been apoplectic about the move, while shareholders are still trying to price in exactly what the scandals and Huang’s departure will mean for the company’s future. But what if Huang comes back?

Industry observers have likened such a possibility to when Steve Jobs left Apple and later returned, though he did so without the cloud of alleged Chinese spies and romantic relationships that violated company conduct standards hanging over his head. New reporting claims that Huang has been working with a crisis PR firm for nearly a year to try to do damage control on the inevitable outing of his relationship with Megaspeed associate Alice Huang. Did things go off-script or is this all part of a larger plan by Huang to not go as quietly as it may have first seemed?

Bloomberg recently reported that the current swirl of scandals had left the founder feeling “depleted.” He had allegedly even taken to making self-flagellating remarks. “Huangâs usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and heâd started using phrases like ‘whatever’ and ‘I donât care,'” it wrote. “I’m a piece of shit” was apparently another thing some heard him say at some point.

But The Financial Times now suggests Huang may be plotting an attempted return. It claims he recently spoke with confidants about the possibility of mounting a comeback at Nvidia. Some allies were even reportedly setting up a “war room” to work on selling that narrative to the company’s board and shareholders. More baseless speculation from randos in Huang’s orbit, or is it all a necessary part of the fall and rise crisis comms playbook the former CEO is running?

Nvidia is set to release its newest quarterly earnings this month, and those are expected to show another astronomical increase in year-over-year profits. The most shocking thing about this entire sordid AI ordeal is not that Huang allegedly had multiple affairs, but that Nvidia’s board was willing to dump the founder so quickly despite his public image and persona being so integral to the company’s underlying brand and recent meteoric success.

Huang basically took Nvidia from gaming graphics backwater to pillar of the global AI economy in just a few years thanks to being in the right place at the right time. Companies have fought much harder to protect much less.

#3699. Ever wanted to play a multiplayer version of Cyberpunk 2077 with your friends? Well, thanks to a mod now in beta, you can

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers."

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

If you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later announced that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

This isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a new mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

Fans of the MMO call for developers to "remove the gold and ban them"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

World of Warcraft: Forever has officially been out in the wild for a good few weeks now, and that's given fans plenty of time to uncover get-rich-quick exploits – including one that's made a good few players especially wealthy… much to the community's dismay.

Dungeons have been an especially hot topic in the community since the MMO left Beta earlier this month, with fan feedback on them leading to a 50% XP boost and further changes as recently as yesterday. The whole experience controversy isn't the only reason dungeons – specifically the Blackmaw Hold – have been in the limelight, though. An exploit that grants folks hundreds of thousands of gold is another.

Blizzard did nerf the exploit this week, which let players burst through enemies for wildly expensive drops in the dungeon over and over again; however, its effects on the economy of WoW: Forever are, unsurprisingly, lasting. So much so, in fact, that those innocent of the exploit's shady dealings are calling for Blizzard to enact a heavier hand. Over on its official forums, for example, one fan writes, "Remove the gold and ban them." They continue: "Remove the gold or I and many others will just quit. This is worse than the bots at this point." Comments see fellow players agreeing with the poster, with the top response reading, "100% the gold needs to be removed and bans need to be handed out." It's not an isolated conversation, either. Threads on Reddit see fans sharing in on the sentiment, with one in particular drawing attention to Blizzard axing the "100+ gold per hour farm."

Replies align well with those on the World of Warcraft forums. "Remove all gold and hand out at minimum a month ban," one exclaims. "Make them miss raid launches or straight up permaban them." They're not the only person to call for a permanent ban here: "If they don't revert gold earned, the economy is already shot with an exploit mafia controlling the market. Remove all gold and ban one month or permaban."

It might seem like a drastic response, but this isn't the first time WoW: Forever fans have had to grapple with gold-related cheating. Back during the beta, Blizzard actually nabbed a good $200 worth of gold off a streamer who was, uh, pretty public with it (spoiler alert: they likely got it via real-money trading, which is strictly forbidden). Prior to that, the studio had stated that its new MMO's economy is "something we're taking very seriously" as well.

So, will we see Blizzard crack down more strongly and dish out some bans to players abusing patched exploits like the Blackmaw Hold one in question here? Only time can tell, I suppose, but I'd argue it'll already have a negative effect on the game's economy by then, sadly.

Blizzard knows World of Warcraft: Forever has a gold problem – but that doesn't mean a feature everyone used to grind it in the OG MMO is coming back

#3697. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.
